procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated September 9, 1968 of the Rajasthan High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 134 of 1968.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants made an application to the High Court of Rajasthan under section 435 read with section 561-A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing the proceedings before the Additional Special Judge and for directing the Special Judge to hand over the appellants to be tried by Court Martial. The High Court dismissed the revision application and directed the Special Judge, Rajasthan to conduct the trial expeditiously.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's order. They contended that the Special Judge had jurisdiction to deal with the State's application and that the Commanding Officer had no power to cancel the intimation dated January 16, 1967. The respondent contended that the effect of the cancellation of the notice dated January 16, 1967, was that no Court Martial proceeding was to be commenced and that in any event the Special Judge had jurisdiction and authority to try and dispose.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Special Judge had jurisdiction to deal with the application of the State and proceed with the trial.

facts: The case was pending before the Special Judge before June 30, 1966.
The case involved both military personnel (the appellants) and three civilians.

On January 17, 1967, the Special Judge noted that the civilians could not be tried by a Court Martial and that there was a potential limitation issue for initiating Court Martial proceedings under the Army Act.
The Special Judge requested the Commanding Officer to refer the matter to the Central Government to resolve the potential jurisdictional conflict.
The competent military authority never formally requested the criminal court to deliver the appellants and ultimately formed the opinion that they should be tried by the Special Court.
No Court Martial proceeding was actually pending against the appellants.
law: Under the Criminal Law Amendment (Amending) Act, 1966, a case pending before a Special Judge before June 30, 1966, is to be tried and disposed of by that Judge.
Civilians charged with an offence alongside military personnel cannot be tried by a Court Martial.
application: The Court determined that since the case was pending before the Special Judge prior to June 30, 1966, the Criminal Law Amendment (Amending) Act, 1966, explicitly granted the Special Judge jurisdiction to try and dispose of it.

The Court found the Special Judge's actions on January 17, 1967, to be justified. Given that civilians were co-accused, it was appropriate for the Judge to ask the military to seek clarification from the Central Government to prevent a conflict of jurisdiction.
The fact that the military authorities never demanded custody and indicated that the appellants should be tried by the Special Court further supported the Special Judge's authority to proceed.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Special Judge had jurisdiction to deal with the State's application and proceed with the trial. This was because the case was pending before the cut-off date stipulated by the Criminal Law Amendment (Amending) Act, 1966, and because the Judge's actions were justified in light of the co-accused civilians and the military's eventual deference to the Special Court's authority.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Commanding Officer, having once intimated that a Court-Martial would be instituted, had the power to cancel that intimation.

facts: On January 16, 1967, the Commanding Officer (CO) informed the Special Judge that four appellants would be tried by Court-Martial.

The Special Judge, noting potential issues like the statute of limitations under the Army Act and the presence of civilian co-accused, requested the CO to refer the matter to the Central Government to resolve the jurisdictional conflict.
In response, on January 28, 1967, the CO wrote to the Special Judge and cancelled the previous notice from January 16.
The appellants challenged this cancellation, arguing that the CO had no power to revoke the initial decision to hold a Court-Martial.
law: Rule 5 of the Criminal Courts and Court Martial (Adjustment of Jurisdiction) Rules, 1952, allows a Commanding Officer to exercise discretion and decide to try an accused by Court-Martial.
Rule 9 of the same rules applies when the military authority is of the opinion that the offender ought to be tried by a criminal court.
application: The Supreme Court found the appellants' argument that the CO's discretion, once exercised, could not be cancelled to be "unacceptable."

The Court reasoned that the CO's decision to cancel the notice was a valid exercise of discretion, made after considering the facts and circumstances, particularly the issues raised by the Special Judge.
By cancelling the notice, the CO effectively expressed the opinion that the appellants should be tried by the criminal court, which resolved the conflict of jurisdiction.
The Court also noted that there were no allegations of bad faith or abuse of power in the CO's decision to cancel the notice.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Commanding Officer did have the power to cancel the initial intimation to institute a Court-Martial. The cancellation was a proper exercise of discretion in light of the circumstances presented by the Special Judge.

issue.issue_text: Whether for a case to be considered 'pending' under Section 5(1)(a) of the 1966 Act, it is necessary for charges to have been formally framed against the accused.

facts: The case involved appellants who were subject to military law and were being tried along with civilians (persons not subject to military law).
This situation brought the case under the purview of Section 5(1)(a) of the Criminal Law Amendment (Amending) Act, 1966.
law: Section 5(1)(a) of the 1966 Act applies to cases pending before a Special Judge where military personnel are "charged with and tried for an offence" together with non-military persons.
Section 5(1)(b) of the 1966 Act applies to cases involving only military personnel and explicitly requires that "charges should also have been framed" for the case to be considered pending.
application: The Court's primary reasoning was based on a direct comparison between the language used in clauses (a) and (b) of Section 5(1).
It noted that clause (a) uses the phrase "charged with", while clause (b) uses the more specific phrase "charges have already been framed".

The Court reasoned that the legislature's use of different wording in two distinct, adjacent clauses was intentional. The absence of the specific requirement for "framing of charges" in clause (a) indicates that it was not intended to be a prerequisite for that clause.

The Court interpreted the words "charged with" in Section 5(1)(a) to mean that there are simply "accusations and allegations" against a person, which is a broader and earlier stage than the formal framing of charges by a court.

Therefore, the Court concluded that the legislative intent was clear: for a mixed case involving military and non-military persons under clause (a), a case is pending as long as accusations have been made, even if formal charges have not yet been framed.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that it is not necessary for charges to have been formally framed for a case to be considered 'pending' under Section 5(1)(a) of the 1966 Act. The Court distinguished the phrase 'charged with' in clause (a) from the explicit requirement that 'charges have already been framed' in clause (b), concluding the former simply means that accusations or allegations have been made against the person.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Special Judge had jurisdiction to deal with the application of the State and proceed with the trial.
appellant_arguments: The appellants contended that they should be delivered to the Army authorities for Court-Martial proceedings, not tried by the Special Judge.
respondent_arguments: The Special Judge had jurisdiction and authority to try the case as it was pending on 30th June, 1966, under the Criminal Law Amendment (Amending) Act, 1966.
The Army authorities indicated that the Special Judge should proceed with the case and did not want the appellants delivered to them for Court-Martial.
The Special Judge was justified in requesting the competent military authority to make a reference to the Central Government.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Commanding Officer, having once intimated that a Court-Martial would be instituted, had the power to cancel that intimation.
appellant_arguments: The appellants argued that they should be tried by Court-Martial as initially intimated by the Commanding Officer.
respondent_arguments: The Army authorities (including the Commanding Officer) ultimately indicated that the Special Judge should proceed with the case and that there would be no Court-Martial proceedings, effectively cancelling the initial intimation.

arguments.issue_text: Whether for a case to be considered 'pending' under Section 5(1)(a) of the 1966 Act, it is necessary for charges to have been formally framed against the accused.
appellant_arguments: The words 'charged with and tried for an offence' in Section 5(1)(a) mean that charges must have been actually framed and the trial commenced.
respondent_arguments: The phrase 'charged with' in Section 5(1)(a) simply means there are accusations and allegations against the person, not that formal charges have been framed.
There is a deliberate distinction between Section 5(1)(a), which uses 'charged with', and Section 5(1)(b), which explicitly requires that 'charges have already been framed'.
The absence of the 'charges framed' requirement in clause (a) shows the legislative intent that it is not a prerequisite for cases falling under that clause.

statutes.act_name: Criminal Courts and Court Martial (Adjustment of Jurisdiction) Rules, 1952

cases.case_name: Ram Sarup v. The Union of India
cases.principle: Section 125 of the Army Act is not unconstitutional or discriminatory because the Act contains sufficient policy to guide the discretion of the officer in choosing between a court-martial and a criminal court.

cases.case_name: Som Datt Datta v. Union of India & Ors.
cases.principle: Sections 125 and 126 of the Army Act provide a satisfactory machinery to resolve jurisdictional conflicts, and Rule 3 of the associated rules applies only after police have completed their investigation and brought the accused before a Magistrate, not when an investigation has merely started.

The case was cited for its examination of the Criminal Courts and Court Martial (Adjustment of Jurisdiction) Rules, 1952, and for the principle that a Judge must proceed in accordance with the provisions of those Rules.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a statute uses distinct phrases in separate but related clauses, such as "charged with" versus "charges have already been framed," the different wording signifies a different legislative intent; "charged with" refers to the existence of accusations and allegations, not the formal framing of charges. A case is considered pending before a court until it is concluded. Furthermore, an authority's exercise of discretion is not irrevocable and can be cancelled, absent any allegations of bad faith or abuse of power.
obiter: There are no allegations of mala fide or abuse of power to challenge the propriety of the exercise of power and discretion.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Special Judge had proper jurisdiction to proceed with the trial because the Commanding Officer's initial intimation to hold a Court-Martial was not an irrevocable decision and was validly cancelled. The discretion to demand a Court-Martial can be withdrawn, and in the absence of any allegations of bad faith or abuse of power, the court will not interfere with that revised decision. Furthermore, the case was legally considered 'pending' before the relevant date, as the test for pendency is simply whether any proceedings can be taken in the cause before the court, not whether formal charges have been framed.
legal_tests_applied: The test for whether a case is 'pending' is whether any proceedings can be taken in the cause before the court or tribunal where it is said to be pending; a case is pending until it is concluded.
A challenge to the propriety of the exercise of an officer's power and discretion requires allegations of 'malafide or abuse of power'.
why_appellant_lost: The contention that the Commanding Officer, having once exercised his discretion to institute a Court-Martial, could not cancel that discretion was found to be unacceptable.

The appellants made no allegations of 'malafide or abuse of power' that would be necessary to challenge the propriety of the Commanding Officer's decision to cancel the initial intimation for a Court-Martial.
The court rejected the narrow interpretation that a case is only 'pending' after charges have been formally framed, applying a broader test instead.
why_respondent_won: The Special Judge was justified in asking the Officer Commanding to make a reference to the Central Government for clarification, particularly because civilian co-accused were involved who could not be tried by Court-Martial.

The Officer Commanding, upon consideration of the facts and the communication from the Special Judge, validly cancelled the previous letter and expressed the opinion that the appellants should be tried by the criminal court.
The case met the legal test for being 'pending' because the court had taken cognizance of it and proceedings could be taken in the cause, which is all that is required.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning supports practical coordination between civilian and military justice systems, especially in cases involving both military personnel and civilians, by allowing authorities to reconsider jurisdictional choices to ensure a proper and unified trial.

The High Court's direction that the Special Judge conduct the trial expeditiously reflects a judicial policy concern for timely justice, especially when significant time has already passed since the charge-sheet was submitted.
